questiontext.text: A predicate is in Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF) when it is written as:

answer.text: A disjunction (OR) of product terms, where each term is a conjunction (AND) of literals

feedback.text: Correct — DNF is a "sum of products": an OR of AND-terms.

answer.text: A conjunction (AND) of sum terms, where each term is a disjunction of literals

feedback.text: That is Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF), a product of sums.

answer.text: A single product term of every variable

feedback.text: That is a minterm, only one special case of a DNF.

answer.text: Any boolean expression, regardless of structure

feedback.text: DNF is a specific normal form, not an arbitrary expression.

generalfeedback.text: DNF (sum of products) writes f as an OR of product terms; each product term is an AND of literals. Notation used here: AND = adjacency (ab), OR = +, NOT = ! (e.g. !a).

questiontext.text: In DNF, a literal is:

answer.text: A variable or its negation (e.g. a or !a)

feedback.text: Correct — a literal is one occurrence of a variable, possibly negated.

answer.text: A conjunction of two or more variables

feedback.text: That is a product term, not a single literal.
That is the entire DNF, not a literal.

answer.text: An assignment of values to all variables

feedback.text: That is a test point/row, not a literal.

generalfeedback.text: A literal is a single variable or its negation, e.g. a or !a. Literals are AND-ed together to form product terms.

questiontext.text: In DNF, a term (product term) is:

answer.text: A conjunction (AND) of one or more literals, e.g. a!bc

feedback.text: Correct — a term is literals AND-ed together.

answer.text: A disjunction (OR) of literals, e.g. a + b + c

feedback.text: That is a sum term (used in CNF), not a DNF product term.
A single variable is one valid term, but terms may AND several literals.

answer.text: The negation of the whole predicate

feedback.text: That is ¬f, not a product term.

generalfeedback.text: A product term is a conjunction of literals, such as a!bc. A DNF is a disjunction (sum) of such product terms.

questiontext.text: For a predicate over the variables a, b, c, a minterm is:

answer.text: A product term that contains every variable exactly once (each as a or !a), e.g. a!bc

feedback.text: Correct — a minterm mentions all variables and is true at exactly one row.

answer.text: A product term that omits at least one variable, e.g. ac

feedback.text: That is a valid product term, but not a minterm — a minterm names every variable.

answer.text: A disjunction of all variables, e.g. a + b + c

feedback.text: That is a sum term, not a minterm.

answer.text: The smallest implicant of the predicate

feedback.text: Size of an implicant is unrelated; a minterm is defined by naming every variable.

generalfeedback.text: A minterm is a product term mentioning every variable exactly once; it is true at exactly one assignment (one truth-table row). Over 3 variables, a!bc is a minterm.

questiontext.text: A product term i is an implicant of predicate f when:

answer.text: Whenever i is true, f is also true (i implies f)

feedback.text: Correct — an implicant implies the predicate.

answer.text: Whenever f is true, i is also true

feedback.text: That is the reverse implication and is not what "implicant" means.

answer.text: i and f are true on exactly the same rows

feedback.text: That would make i logically equivalent to f, which is stronger than being an implicant.
An implicant makes f true, not false.

generalfeedback.text: An implicant is a product term that implies f: every assignment satisfying the term also satisfies f. Each term listed in a DNF of f is an implicant of f.

questiontext.text: A prime implicant of f is:

answer.text: An implicant from which no single literal can be removed while it stays an implicant

feedback.text: Correct — it is a "maximal" (irreducible) implicant.

answer.text: An implicant that contains every variable

feedback.text: That describes a minterm; prime implicants are usually smaller.

answer.text: Any product term appearing in some DNF of f

feedback.text: Such a term is an implicant, but it need not be prime (a literal might still be removable).

answer.text: The disjunction of all implicants of f

feedback.text: That is a DNF of f, not a single prime implicant.

generalfeedback.text: A prime implicant is an implicant that cannot be reduced: dropping any one of its literals yields a term that no longer implies f.

name.text: What is a unique true point

questiontext.text: A unique true point (UTP) for an implicant i of f is an assignment that:

answer.text: Makes i true and every other implicant of f false

feedback.text: Correct — at a UTP, i alone is responsible for f being true.

answer.text: Makes i true, regardless of the other implicants

feedback.text: That is just a true point of i; a UTP additionally requires all other implicants to be false.
A UTP is a true point: it makes i (and hence f) true.

answer.text: Is the only assignment making f true

feedback.text: "Unique" refers to only one implicant being true, not to f having a single satisfying row.

generalfeedback.text: A UTP for implicant i is an assignment where i is true and all other implicants are false, so i is the unique implicant accounting for f's truth there.

name.text: What is a near false point

questiontext.text: A near false point (NFP) for a literal L of implicant i is an assignment that:

answer.text: Makes f false, but flipping only literal L makes i (and f) true

feedback.text: Correct — it lies one literal away from a true point of i.

answer.text: Makes f true using implicant i

feedback.text: An NFP makes f false, not true.

answer.text: Makes every literal of i false at once

feedback.text: Only the one literal L is "wrong"; the others keep the values that would make i true.

answer.text: Differs from a true point of i in two or more variables

feedback.text: An NFP differs in exactly one variable — the one for literal L — hence "near".

generalfeedback.text: A near false point for literal L of implicant i makes f false, yet flipping just the variable of L turns i (and f) true. It sits one variable away from making i true.

name.text: Count product terms in ab + cd

questiontext.text: How many product terms does the DNF ab + cd contain?

feedback.text: Correct — the two terms are ab and cd.
4 is the number of literals, not the number of terms.
The + separates two distinct product terms.
There are exactly two terms, ab and cd.

generalfeedback.text: ab + cd is a disjunction of two product terms, ab and cd, so it has 2 terms (each an implicant of the predicate).

questiontext.text: How many literal occurrences does the DNF ab + cd contain?

feedback.text: Correct — a, b, c, d each appear once.
2 is the number of terms, not the number of literals.
There are only four literal occurrences: a, b, c, d.
Count each literal in each term: ab has 2, cd has 2, total 4.

generalfeedback.text: Term ab contributes literals a and b; term cd contributes c and d — four literal occurrences in all.

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a single literal?

feedback.text: Correct — !b is a variable's negation, a literal.
ab is a product term (two literals AND-ed), not a single literal.
a + b is a disjunction of two literals, not a single literal.
a!bc is a product term of three literals.

generalfeedback.text: A literal is one variable or its negation. !b qualifies; ab and a!bc are product terms and a + b is a disjunction.

questiontext.text: How many literal occurrences does the DNF ab + c contain?

feedback.text: Correct — a and b in the first term, c in the second.
2 is the number of terms; there are 3 literal occurrences.
Only a, b, and c appear — three literals.
Count all literals across both terms: 2 + 1 = 3.

generalfeedback.text: Term ab has literals a and b; term c has literal c — three literal occurrences total.

questiontext.text: How many distinct variables (clauses) does the predicate ab + cd involve?

feedback.text: Correct — a, b, c, and d.
2 is the number of terms; the predicate uses 4 distinct variables.
16 = 2^4 is the number of truth-table rows, not the number of variables.
There are 4 distinct variables: a, b, c, d.

generalfeedback.text: The predicate mentions a, b, c, d — four distinct variables, giving 2^4 = 16 truth-table rows.

questiontext.text: A prime implicant is an implicant from which no single literal can be removed while it remains an implicant.

feedback.text: Correct — that irreducibility is exactly what makes an implicant prime.
Prime implicants are precisely the irreducible implicants; removing any literal breaks the implication.

generalfeedback.text: An implicant is prime when it is minimal: dropping any one literal produces a term that no longer implies f.

questiontext.text: Every product term appearing in a DNF of f is an implicant of f.

feedback.text: Correct — if a term is true, that whole disjunct is true, so f is true; the term implies f.
Each disjunct, when true, forces the OR (and thus f) to be true, so every DNF term implies f.

generalfeedback.text: Because f is the OR of its terms, any term being true makes f true. Hence every term of a DNF of f is (by definition) an implicant of f.

name.text: UTP for ab in ab + c

questiontext.text: For f = ab + c (variable order a,b,c), which assignment is a unique true point for the implicant ab?

feedback.text: Correct — ab is true and c is false, so ab is the only true implicant.
At 111 the implicant c is also true, so ab is not the unique true implicant.
Here ab is false (b=0), so this is not even a true point of ab.
ab is false here; this is a true point of c, not of ab.

generalfeedback.text: A UTP for ab needs ab true and every other implicant (here c) false: a=1, b=1, c=0, i.e. 110. It is the only UTP for ab in this predicate.

name.text: UTP for c in ab + c

questiontext.text: For f = ab + c (order a,b,c), which assignment is a unique true point for the implicant c?

feedback.text: Correct — c is true and ab is false, so c is the only true implicant.
Here ab is also true, so c is not the unique true implicant.
c is false here (c=0); this is a true point of ab, not of c.
f is false here, so it is not a true point at all.

generalfeedback.text: c has three UTPs — 001, 011, 101 — each with c true and ab false. Of the options, only 001 qualifies (111 also makes ab true).

name.text: NFP for literal a of ab in ab + c

questiontext.text: For f = ab + c (order a,b,c), which assignment is a near false point for literal a of the implicant ab?

feedback.text: Correct — f is false here, and flipping a to 1 gives 110, making ab (and f) true.
f is false here, but flipping a gives 000, where ab is still false (b=0). Not an NFP for a.
f is true here (ab holds), so it is a true point, not a near false point.
f is true here (c holds), so it cannot be a near false point.

generalfeedback.text: An NFP for literal a of ab needs f false and the flip of a alone to make ab true. That requires b=1, c=0, a=0: assignment 010. Flipping a yields 110 with ab true.

questiontext.text: At a unique true point the predicate f is ____, and at a near false point f is ____.

feedback.text: Correct — a UTP is a true point of f; an NFP is a false point of f.
Reversed — the UTP makes f true and the NFP makes f false.
An NFP makes f false, not true.
A UTP makes f true, not false.

generalfeedback.text: By definition, a UTP makes its implicant (hence f) true, while an NFP makes f false but is one literal flip away from making an implicant true.

questiontext.text: Consider f = ab + a!b, which simplifies to a. Which statement is correct?

answer.text: Neither ab nor a!b is a prime implicant, because in each the second literal can be dropped (a alone still implies f)

feedback.text: Correct — since f = a, the term a is an implicant, so ab and a!b are both reducible.

answer.text: Both ab and a!b are prime implicants

feedback.text: Neither is prime: removing b (or !b) leaves a, which still implies f.

answer.text: Only ab is a prime implicant

feedback.text: ab is reducible to a, so it is not prime.

answer.text: a is not an implicant of f

feedback.text: Since f = a, the term a implies f — it is in fact the only prime implicant.

generalfeedback.text: f = ab + a!b = a. The single prime implicant is a. Both listed terms carry a removable literal, so neither is prime.

name.text: Number of UTPs UTPC requires for ab + cd

questiontext.text: For f = ab + cd, how many unique true points must Unique True Point Coverage (UTPC) require (one per implicant)?

feedback.text: Correct — one UTP for ab and one for cd.
4 is the literal count; UTPC needs one UTP per implicant, and there are 2 implicants.
Each implicant needs its own UTP, and no single point can be a UTP for both.
7 is the number of true rows; UTPC requires one UTP per implicant, i.e. 2.

generalfeedback.text: UTPC requires a UTP for each implicant. With two implicants (ab, cd), it requires 2 unique true points; since a UTP makes only its own implicant true, one test cannot serve both.

name.text: Number of NFPs NFPC requires for ab + cd

questiontext.text: For f = ab + cd, how many near false points must Near False Point Coverage (NFPC) require (one per literal of each implicant)?

feedback.text: Correct — one NFP for each of the four literals a, b, c, d.
2 is the implicant count; NFPC requires one NFP per literal, and there are 4 literals.
There are only 4 literal occurrences, so 4 NFPs are required.
16 = 2^4 is the row count, not the number of NFPs required.

generalfeedback.text: NFPC requires a near false point for each literal of each implicant. Terms ab and cd have four literals total (a, b, c, d), so 4 NFPs are required.

questiontext.text: For f = !ab + ac (order a,b,c), which assignment is a unique true point for the implicant !ab?

feedback.text: Correct — !ab is true (a=0, b=1) and ac is false (a=0), so !ab is the unique true implicant.
!ab is false here because a=1, so !a is false.
Here ac is true and !ab is false (a=1); not a UTP for !ab.
!ab is false here because b=0.

generalfeedback.text: !ab needs a=0 and b=1; to keep ac false we need a=0 (already) — so both 010 and 011 are UTPs. Of the options only 010 qualifies.

name.text: NFP for literal c of ac in !ab + ac

questiontext.text: For f = !ab + ac (order a,b,c), which assignment is a near false point for literal c of the implicant ac?

feedback.text: Correct — f is false here, and flipping c to 1 gives 101, making ac (and f) true.
f is true here (ac holds), so it is a true point, not a near false point.
f is false, but flipping c gives 001, where ac is still false (a=0). Not an NFP for c.
f is true here (!ab holds), so it cannot be a near false point.

generalfeedback.text: An NFP for c of ac needs f false and flipping c alone to make ac true, i.e. a=1 and c=0. With a=1, !ab is false; b may be 0 or 1. 100 works: flipping c yields 101 with ac true.

questiontext.text: For f = ac + bc (order a,b,c), at the assignment 111 (a=1, b=1, c=1), how many of the two implicants are true?

answer.text: 2 — both ac and bc are true

feedback.text: Correct — with a=b=c=1, both terms hold, so 111 is not a unique true point for either.
bc is also true at 111 (b=1, c=1).
Both terms are true; f is true at 111.

answer.text: It depends on the variable order

feedback.text: Truth values do not depend on the order in which variables are written.

generalfeedback.text: At 111 both ac and bc are true, so 111 is a shared true point — it cannot be a UTP for either implicant. The overlap is why unique true points must be chosen carefully.

name.text: Single test for Implicant Coverage of ab + cd

questiontext.text: Can a single test satisfy Implicant Coverage (IC) for f = ab + cd?

answer.text: Yes — the assignment 1111 makes both ab and cd true at once

feedback.text: Correct — IC only asks that each implicant be true in some test, and 1111 makes both true.

answer.text: No — IC always needs one test per implicant

feedback.text: That is UTPC. Plain IC can reuse a single test if it makes every implicant true.

answer.text: No — a single test can never make two product terms true

feedback.text: 1111 makes both ab and cd true simultaneously.

answer.text: Yes, but only under Combinatorial Coverage

feedback.text: Feasibility of one test for IC does not depend on any other criterion.

generalfeedback.text: IC requires each implicant to be made true by some test — the same test may serve several. At 1111 both ab and cd are true, so one test satisfies IC. UTPC, by contrast, forbids this by demanding each true point be unique to one implicant.

name.text: UTP for a in a + bc

questiontext.text: For f = a + bc (order a,b,c), which assignment is a unique true point for the implicant a?

feedback.text: Correct — a is true and bc is false, so a is the unique true implicant.
bc is also true here, so a is not the unique true implicant.
a is false here; this is a true point of bc, not of a.
f is false here, so it is not a true point.

generalfeedback.text: a has UTPs 100, 101, 110 (a true, bc false). 111 fails because bc is also true. Of the options, 100 is the UTP.

name.text: Is a an implicant of ab + cd

questiontext.text: The single literal a is an implicant of f = ab + cd.

feedback.text: Correct — at a=1, b=0, c=0, d=0 (1000) the term a is true but f is false, so a does not imply f.
Counterexample 1000: a is true yet f = ab + cd is false, so a does not imply f.

generalfeedback.text: For a to be an implicant, every assignment with a=1 must make f true. But 1000 has a=1 and f=0, so a is not an implicant of ab + cd.

questiontext.text: An assignment at which implicant i is true but at least one other implicant of f is also true is:

answer.text: A true point of f, but not a unique true point for i

feedback.text: Correct — uniqueness fails because more than one implicant is true.

answer.text: A unique true point for i

feedback.text: A UTP requires all other implicants to be false; here another one is true.

answer.text: A near false point for i

feedback.text: An NFP makes f false; this point makes f true.

answer.text: Not a true point of f at all

feedback.text: Since i is true, f is true, so it is a true point — just not a unique one.

generalfeedback.text: It is a true point of f (i is true), but not a UTP for i because another implicant is simultaneously true, so i is not the unique cause of f's truth.

name.text: Truth value of f at a near false point

questiontext.text: At a near false point, the predicate f must evaluate to:

feedback.text: Correct — an NFP is a false point of f that is one literal flip away from a true point.
That would be a true point; an NFP makes f false.

answer.text: either true or false, depending on the implicant

feedback.text: By definition an NFP always makes f false.
f is a total boolean function; it is defined at every assignment.

generalfeedback.text: A near false point makes f false; flipping the one targeted literal turns the implicant (and f) true. The "false" value at the NFP is essential to the pairing used by CUTPNFP.

name.text: CUTPNFP pair for literal a of ab

questiontext.text: For f = ab + cd (order a,b,c,d), a CUTPNFP pair for literal a of implicant ab is a unique true point and a near false point that differ in exactly variable a. Which pair works?

feedback.text: Correct — they differ only in a; 1100 makes ab (only) true, 0100 makes f false and flips to true when a is set.
These differ in variable b, not a — that is the pair for literal b.
These differ in multiple variables, so they do not isolate literal a.
0011 is a UTP for cd, not for ab, so it does not pair with an NFP for literal a of ab.

generalfeedback.text: For literal a of ab: UTP 1100 (ab uniquely true) and NFP 0100 (f false) differ only in a; setting a at the NFP restores ab and f. This isolates a's independent effect.

name.text: CUTPNFP pair for literal b of ab

questiontext.text: For f = ab + cd (order a,b,c,d), which UTP/NFP pair isolates literal b of implicant ab (differ in exactly variable b)?

feedback.text: Correct — they differ only in b; 1000 makes f false, and setting b restores ab and f.
These differ in a, not b — that is the pair for literal a.
1110 and 1000 differ in variables b and c, so they do not isolate b alone.
1000 makes f false, so it is not a UTP; the roles are also reversed.

generalfeedback.text: For literal b of ab: UTP 1100 and NFP 1000 differ only in b. At 1000 f is false; setting b to 1 restores ab (and f), demonstrating b's independent effect.

name.text: Number of CUTPNFP pairs for ab + cd

questiontext.text: For f = ab + cd, how many corresponding (UTP, NFP) pairs does CUTPNFP require — one per literal of each implicant?

feedback.text: Correct — one pair for each of the four literals a, b, c, d.
2 counts implicants; CUTPNFP pairs are per literal, so there are 4.
There are 4 literals, hence 4 pairs, not 8.
7 is the number of true rows, unrelated to the pair count.

generalfeedback.text: CUTPNFP forms one UTP/NFP pair per literal of each implicant. With literals a, b (in ab) and c, d (in cd), that is 4 pairs.

name.text: Why 111 is not a UTP in ac + bc

questiontext.text: For f = ac + bc (order a,b,c), why is 111 not a unique true point for the implicant ac?

answer.text: Because the other implicant bc is also true at 111

feedback.text: Correct — with b=1, c=1 the term bc is true too, so ac is not the unique true implicant.
ac is true at 111 (a=1, c=1); the problem is that bc is true as well.
f is true at 111; it just is not uniquely due to ac.

answer.text: Because 111 is a near false point

feedback.text: 111 makes f true, so it is not a near false point.

generalfeedback.text: At 111 both ac and bc are true, so ac is not the sole cause of f's truth. The unique true point for ac is 101 (ac true, bc false).

name.text: The unique true point for ac in ac + bc

questiontext.text: For f = ac + bc (order a,b,c), which assignment is the (only) unique true point for the implicant ac?

feedback.text: Correct — ac is true and bc is false (b=0), so ac is the unique true implicant.
bc is also true here, so ac is not unique.
ac is false here (c=0), so f is false.
ac is false here (a=0); f is false.

generalfeedback.text: ac is true only when a=1 and c=1; to make bc false we need b=0. That forces 101 — the sole unique true point for ac.

name.text: DNF of not-f for ab + c

questiontext.text: MUTPC/MNFPC also work with the DNF of ¬f. For f = ab + c, which is a correct DNF of ¬f?

feedback.text: Correct — ¬f is true exactly when c=0 and not(ab), i.e. !c(!a + !b).
This is true at 110 (where f is true), so it is not ¬f.
This covers only 000; ¬f is also true at 010 and 100.
This is true at 100 and 010, but f itself is false there, and it misses 000 — it is not ¬f.

generalfeedback.text: f = ab + c is false exactly on 000, 010, 100 — all with c=0 and ab false. So ¬f = !c(!a + !b) = !a!c + !b!c.

name.text: Prime implicants of not-f for ab + cd

questiontext.text: For f = ab + cd, the negation is ¬f = (!a + !b)(!c + !d). In minimal DNF, how many prime implicants does ¬f have?

feedback.text: Correct — expanding gives !a!c + !a!d + !b!c + !b!d, four prime implicants.
The product (!a + !b)(!c + !d) expands to four product terms, not two.
¬f is not a single product term; it expands to four.
7 is the number of true rows of f; ¬f has 9 true rows and 4 prime implicants.

generalfeedback.text: Distributing (!a + !b)(!c + !d) yields !a!c + !a!d + !b!c + !b!d — four prime implicants, each a valid implicant of ¬f. MUTPC would require UTPs for the implicants of both f and ¬f.

questiontext.text: Over the 8 assignments of a,b,c, how many make f = ab + c true?

feedback.text: Correct — the 4 rows with c=1, plus 110 (a=1,b=1,c=0).
c=1 already gives 4 true rows; 110 adds a fifth.
Recount: exactly 5 rows are true (001,011,101,110,111).
Too few — c=1 alone yields 4 true rows.

generalfeedback.text: f is true whenever c=1 (4 rows) or ab=1 (adds 110). The true rows are 001, 011, 101, 110, 111 — five in all.

questiontext.text: Over the 16 assignments of a,b,c,d, how many make f = ab + cd true?

feedback.text: Correct — 3 rows with ab (cd false) + 3 with cd (ab false) + 1 with both (1111) = 7.
Adding the two blocks of 4 double-counts 1111; the true count is 7.
Recount — there are 7 true rows.
ab alone gives 4 rows and cd gives 4 more (overlapping in 1111), for 7 distinct rows.

generalfeedback.text: ab is true on 4 rows and cd on 4 rows; they share only 1111, so by inclusion–exclusion 4 + 4 − 1 = 7 assignments make f true.

questiontext.text: A test suite that satisfies only Unique True Point Coverage (UTPC) is guaranteed to make f evaluate to false in at least one test.

feedback.text: Correct — every UTP makes its implicant (and f) true, so a UTPC-only suite may never make f false.
All unique true points make f true; nothing in UTPC forces a false point, so f need never be false.

generalfeedback.text: Each UTP is a true point of f. A suite consisting solely of UTPs makes f true in every test, so UTPC alone does not guarantee a false evaluation — it does not subsume Predicate Coverage.

questiontext.text: A test suite that satisfies only Near False Point Coverage (NFPC) is guaranteed to make f evaluate to true in at least one test.

feedback.text: Correct — every near false point makes f false, so an NFPC-only suite may never make f true.
All near false points make f false; nothing in NFPC forces a true point, so f need never be true.

generalfeedback.text: Each NFP is a false point of f. A suite of only NFPs makes f false in every test, so NFPC alone does not guarantee a true evaluation — it does not subsume Predicate Coverage on its own.

questiontext.text: Because CUTPNFP includes a unique true point (f true) and a near false point (f false) for each literal, any CUTPNFP-satisfying suite makes f both true and false — so it subsumes Predicate Coverage.

feedback.text: Correct — the UTPs give a true evaluation and the NFPs give a false one, covering both values of f.
CUTPNFP requires both UTPs (f true) and NFPs (f false), so f necessarily takes both values.

generalfeedback.text: CUTPNFP pairs a UTP (f true) with an NFP (f false) for every literal. The suite therefore contains at least one true and one false evaluation of f, satisfying Predicate Coverage.

questiontext.text: Unique True Point Coverage (UTPC) subsumes Implicant Coverage (IC).

feedback.text: Correct — a UTP for implicant i makes i true, so covering a UTP for each implicant also makes each implicant true, which is exactly IC.
Every UTP makes its own implicant true; requiring one per implicant satisfies IC, so UTPC subsumes IC.

generalfeedback.text: IC requires each implicant to be made true by some test. A UTP for implicant i makes i true, so a UTPC suite (a UTP per implicant) automatically satisfies IC.

questiontext.text: What does a CUTPNFP (UTP, NFP) pair for a literal L demonstrate?

answer.text: That toggling only L flips f — L's independent effect on the outcome (the DNF analog of MC/DC)

feedback.text: Correct — the pair differs only in L and f changes, showing L independently affects f.

answer.text: That all 2^n combinations of variables are exercised

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage, far more than CUTPNFP requires.

answer.text: That the predicate is always true

feedback.text: The NFP of the pair makes f false, so f is not always true.

answer.text: That L never affects the outcome

feedback.text: The pair shows exactly the opposite: L does affect f.

generalfeedback.text: A CUTPNFP pair is a UTP and an NFP differing only in literal L; f is true at one and false at the other, so flipping L alone flips f. This mirrors MC/DC's independent-effect requirement in DNF form.

name.text: Missing near false point in ab + a!b

questiontext.text: For f = ab + a!b (which equals a), literal b of the implicant ab has no near false point. Why?

answer.text: Any point where flipping b would make ab true already has a=1, so f = a is already true there — f is never false at such a point

feedback.text: Correct — the required "f false" condition cannot hold, so no NFP for b exists.

answer.text: Because b does not appear in the predicate

feedback.text: b does appear in the term ab; the issue is that ab is redundant (f = a).

answer.text: Because ab has no unique true point

feedback.text: ab does have a UTP (11); the missing NFP is a separate consequence of redundancy.
f = a is not a tautology; it is false whenever a=0.

generalfeedback.text: An NFP for b of ab needs f false while flipping b makes ab true — but making ab true by flipping b requires a=1, and with a=1 f = a is already true. No assignment satisfies both, so this NFP is infeasible: NFPC can be infeasible for a non-prime (redundant) implicant.
